unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 2! In this unit you explore the natural world and the weather. You learn to name places in nature — canyons, meadows and bays — and to talk about weather, from a foggy morning to a powerful hurricane. You compare two things, say which is the greatest, state science facts, and ask questions like a real scientist. You read about weather around the world, listen to a weather report, speak about the world around you, and write your own weather facts, instructions and poem. By the end you can explain how weather works and how to stay safe, just as Amal and Nora do in this unit's story.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the Vocabulary section and learn a few weather and nature words each day.
Work through the six grammar lessons, which carry all eight patterns from the source, and complete every practice.
Read the story “The Storm and the Science Tent”, then answer the comprehension questions.
Work through the four skills in order: Reading & Listening, Speaking, Writing, Activities.
Take the Nature & Weather checkpoint quiz, then finish with the Self-Assessment.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: The air you take in and let out of your lungs.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: I took a deep breath before I started to speak.
practiceSentences: Amal takes a deep breath before she reads her poem aloud.
Nora took a slow breath and dived into the pool.
How long can you hold your breath underwater?

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult beside me, ask me what breath means and have me use it in a sentence about running.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: The clear water that comes from your skin when you are hot.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: After running in the sun, I wiped the sweat from my face.
practiceSentences: Cool water helps when sweat runs down your face on hot days.

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult listening, ask me to explain how sweat cools the body, then check my answer.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A small amount of water in the air or on a surface.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The grass was wet with moisture after the rain.
practiceSentences: Plants pull moisture from the soil through their thin roots.

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me, while an adult is nearby, to say where moisture comes from and to compare it with sweat.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: The top or outside part of something.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The surface of the lake was calm and shiny.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: The soft hair that covers some animals' bodies.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Animals use their thick fur to stay warm in snowy weather.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A deep valley with steep sides, often with a river at the bottom.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The canyon was much deeper than the meadow.
practiceSentences: Our class watched a film about the deepest canyon in the world.

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to compare a canyon with a meadow using deeper, while an adult listens to my sentence.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A large field of grass and flowers where animals graze.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A part of the sea or a lake that is partly surrounded by land.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The small boats sailed safely into the bay.
practiceSentences: Fishing boats shelter in the bay when the wind grows strong.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A time of heavy rain, wind, or snow, sometimes with thunder.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Small balls of ice that fall from the sky during a storm.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A very strong storm with heavy wind and rain.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The hurricane blew down many trees.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: h - u - r - r - i - c - a - n - e

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A spinning column of wind that touches the ground and can cause damage.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: t - o - r - n - a - d - o
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult present, ask me to describe how a tornado moves and how it differs from a hurricane.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: When the air is full of tiny water drops and you cannot see far.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: It was a foggy morning, and I could barely see the trees.
practiceSentences: Every foggy morning hides the hills behind a soft grey curtain.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Covered with, or full of, snow.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A mountain that can erupt with hot lava, ash, and gas.

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to tell an adult three facts about a volcano using the present simple for facts.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To do with the sun.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: We used solar power to charge the light.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: The reddish-brown layer that forms on metal when it gets wet.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The old bike was covered in rust after it was left in the rain.

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to explain to an adult why rust forms and how we can stop metal from rusting.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A soft, fuzzy growth that forms on old food or wet things.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: I found some mould on the bread in the kitchen.
practiceSentences: Green mould appeared on the cheese we left out overnight.

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me, with an adult present, to say what mould needs to grow and how we keep food safe.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To move around freely with no set place to go.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Lions roam across the grasslands looking for food.

readings.title: Weather Around the World
readings.setting: Familiar lakeside town and everyday learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Weather is different all around the world. In some places, the air is foggy and grey in the morning, and people walk slowly along the path until the mist begins to lift. In other places, a hot sun makes people sweat, especially where dry canyons stretch for miles under a clear sky. Near a quiet bay or a green meadow, the weather often feels gentler, but even calm places can change quickly once the wind turns.
High in the mountains, snow falls softly and covers the ground in white, while down by the coast, moisture from the sea keeps the air feeling damp all day. Rain helps plants grow, because plants need moisture, so farmers watch the clouds and hope for a steady shower rather than a flood.
Not all weather is gentle. A gentle storm brings rain, but a hurricane brings very strong wind that can bend trees and tear roofs from houses. Sometimes hail rattles down from dark clouds like handfuls of small stones, and in open country a tornado can spin across the land faster than almost anything a person has ever seen.
Weather can be calm, and weather can be wild. Scientists study the wind, the clouds and the temperature every day so that people everywhere can stay safe. Wherever we live, we watch the sky and learn, because understanding the weather helps us plan our days and look after our homes.

readings.title: A Poem: “The Foggy Morning”
readings.setting: A hillside on a foggy morning
readings.passageScript:
The morning air is damp and grey,
The hills have almost gone away.
So still, so quiet, soft and slow —
The whole world hides in fog below.

readings.title: The Weather Report
readings.setting: A local radio weather desk near the lake
readings.passageScript:
“Good morning, listeners! This is your local weather report, coming to you live from the station beside the lake. Here is today's weather. It is foggy near the lake this morning, so please walk slowly and take care on the path until the mist clears.
By midday, the sun will come out, and it will be warm and pleasant for anyone visiting the meadow or the bay. It should be a lovely afternoon for a walk, though the breeze may pick up a little near the water.
But the weather will not stay calm all day. Tonight, a storm may bring rain and hail, so bring your washing in early and make sure your windows are shut tight. The surface of the lake could turn choppy once the wind arrives. Remember: if you hear thunder, go inside and stay calm, and never shelter under a tall tree during a storm.
Tomorrow should be calmer, with light cloud in the morning and clearer skies by the afternoon. Farmers near the canyon fields will be glad of a little extra moisture after such a dry week.
That is all from the weather desk today. Stay safe, and enjoy your day!”

readings.title: Two Friends at the Science Fair
readings.setting: The science fair tent beside the lake
readings.passageScript:
Amal: “Look at our poster! A tornado spins faster than any other storm.”
Nora: “Yes, and a hurricane is stronger than a normal storm. The volcano is the most powerful of all!”
Amal: “I still love the canyon picture best. It shows just how deep a canyon can be, deeper even than the lake.”
Nora: “True, but look at our moisture chart too. It shows how rain forms over the bay and drifts across the meadow.”
Amal: “Do you remember when hail fell on the school roof last week? It rattled like tiny stones for ten whole minutes.”
Nora: “I do! My little brother roamed around the garden afterwards, collecting the biggest pieces before they melted.”
Amal: “We should tell visitors that a storm can be dangerous, but we can stay safe if we watch the sky and listen for thunder.”
Nora: “Good idea. Let's practise our safety facts once more before the judges arrive.”

readings.title: The Storm and the Science Tent
readings.setting: A lakeside town during a spell of strange weather
readings.passageScript:
Every year, Amal looked forward to the school science fair. Her school set up a big tent near the lake. Students shared their projects there with the whole community. This year, Amal and her friend Nora had planned a weather display. They wanted to teach people how storms work and how to stay safe.
On the morning of the fair, the sky already looked strange. A grey, foggy mist covered the path. “I can barely see the ground,” Nora said. “We should walk slowly.”
Amal nodded. “It is the foggiest morning we have had all year.”
When they reached the lake, the tent was ready. Their teacher, Yasmin, was arranging the students' posters. “Set up your display near the solar light,” she said. “The sun is not strong today, but it will still help.”
Nora unrolled their poster about hurricanes, volcanoes and tornadoes. “This one shows a tornado moving across a field,” she said. “It spins faster than any other storm!”
Amal added, “And this picture shows a volcano with hot lava. It is dangerous, but it is also beautiful.”
People began to arrive. Some students talked about meadows, others about the lake or the forest. Amal's younger brother Idris pointed at the display. “What is a canyon?” he asked.
“It is a deep valley,” Amal said. “It is much deeper than a meadow. A river can run through it. A canyon can be the deepest land on Earth.”
Teacher Yasmin clapped her hands. “Time for a safety quiz! Nora, your turn.”
Nora stood up. “What causes a hurricane?” she asked.
Maya raised her hand. “Warm water and strong wind?”
“Correct!” Nora smiled.
“Now Amal,” said Teacher Yasmin.
Amal pointed to a picture. “Where does hail fall from?”
“From the clouds during a storm,” Leo answered.
“Right,” said Amal. “Hail can damage crops, so we must always watch the weather.”
Just then, the wind picked up. The surface of the lake began to ripple. A few parents looked up at the sky.
Suddenly, a man shouted, “It is coming back! The storm from last week!”
Some children began to panic. “Do not run!” Teacher Yasmin said firmly. “Let us all move inside the hall. Quickly, but calmly.”
As they packed their things, Amal felt something cold on her cheek. “Hail!” she said. Small balls of ice bounced on the ground. “Let us go!”
They reached the hall just as the wind began to howl outside. Teacher Yasmin closed the door. “We are safe here,” she said.
Nora sat down, catching her breath. “My heart is beating fast,” she said. Her shirt was wet with sweat.
“That was frightening,” said Amal. “But it was exciting too.”
Inside, they carried on with their weather talk. They showed how animals use thick fur to stay warm in snowy weather. They also showed how moisture in the soil helps plants grow.
“Rust forms when metal gets wet and is left too long,” Nora explained. “Look at that old nail outside.”
“And mould grows on food when we leave it too long,” Amal added. “That is why we always cover our lunch boxes!”
Maya pointed at a chart. “What is that tall tree near the bay?” she asked.
“That is a royal palm tree,” Nora said. “It grows near the water. It is tall and strong, like the tree of a king.”
Amal smiled. “Nature is powerful,” she said, “but we can learn to understand it.”
When the storm finally passed, the sky cleared. Sunshine filled the room. “Look,” Leo said. “The light is shining brightly now.”
Teacher Yasmin smiled. “You all did well today. You learned, you taught, and you stayed calm. You showed real courage.”
Amal and Nora packed up their project. “Even with the storm, this was the most exciting science fair ever,” Amal said.
“And we did not even have to roam far to learn something new,” Nora laughed.
Outside, puddles sparkled in the sun. The wind had slowed, but the lesson had stayed.

comprehension.question: In “Weather Around the World”, why do plants need moisture?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Plants need moisture to grow, and the rain gives them that water.
comprehension.explanation: The text joins the two ideas with because: rain helps plants grow, because plants need moisture.

comprehension.question: Which two words does the text use for the morning air in some places?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The text says the morning air is foggy and grey.
comprehension.explanation: The second sentence pairs the adjectives foggy and grey to picture a dull morning.

comprehension.question: What difference does the text give between a gentle storm and a hurricane?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A gentle storm brings rain, but a hurricane brings very strong wind.
comprehension.explanation: The writer contrasts the two with but, so the hurricane is clearly the more powerful weather.

comprehension.question: Which three words in the poem show that the foggy morning is calm?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The poem uses still, quiet and slow to show the calm.
comprehension.explanation: Line three lists those quiet words together, so the morning sounds hushed and gentle.

comprehension.question: Why does the poet say the hills have almost gone away?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The fog is so thick that the hills cannot be seen from below.
comprehension.explanation: The hills have not moved; the last line explains that the whole world hides in fog.

comprehension.question: According to the weather report, what may the storm bring tonight?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The report says the storm may bring rain and hail tonight.
comprehension.explanation: The presenter gives the night forecast in one sentence, naming both rain and hail.

comprehension.question: What does the reporter tell listeners to do when they hear thunder, and why?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Go inside and stay calm, because thunder warns that the storm is close.
comprehension.explanation: The safety line comes straight after the storm forecast, so the advice belongs to that storm.

comprehension.question: Which storm does Amal say spins faster than any other?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Amal says a tornado spins faster than any other storm.
comprehension.explanation: Amal points at the poster and names the tornado as the fastest spinning storm.

comprehension.question: Nora says “stronger” and “most powerful”. Which one compares only two things?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Stronger compares two things, and most powerful compares many things.
comprehension.explanation: Stronger is a comparative, so it needs two items; most powerful is a superlative for a whole group.

comprehension.question: What did Amal and Nora plan to teach visitors at the science fair?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They planned to teach how storms work and how people can stay safe.
comprehension.explanation: The first paragraph states the pair's purpose before the fair even begins.

comprehension.question: What happened to the lake just before the storm returned?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The wind picked up and the surface of the lake began to ripple.
comprehension.explanation: The ripple is the warning sign; the shout about the storm comes in the next paragraph.

comprehension.question: How can you tell that Nora was frightened once the class reached the hall?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She sat catching her breath, her heart was beating fast and her shirt was wet with sweat.
comprehension.explanation: The writer shows the fear through her body instead of naming the feeling directly.

grammar.title: Comparative Adjectives
grammar.explanation: Comparative adjectives compare two things. They tell us how one thing is more or less than another — bigger, deeper, stronger. They help us describe our world clearly. For example: “A hurricane is stronger than a storm.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Short word (one syllable): add -er. strong → stronger, deep → deeper.
Word ending in -y: change y to i, add -er. happy → happier, foggy → foggier.
Long word (two or more syllables): use more before it. beautiful → more beautiful.
Always use than to join the two things you compare.
Watch out for irregulars: good → better, bad → worse.
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “A hurricane is strong than a storm.” ✗
Fix: Use the comparative form and “than”: “A hurricane is stronger than a storm.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: “-er for one syllable, more for two or more!” Think of the word than as a little bridge that joins the two things you are comparing.
grammar.practice: Write the comparative form of the word in brackets. | An elephant is ______ (big) than a dog. | This test is ______ (easy) than the last one. | Mount Kenya is ______ (high) than that hill. | The canyon is ______ (deep) than the meadow. Answer key: 1) bigger, 2) easier, 3) higher, 4) deeper.

grammar.title: Superlative Adjectives
grammar.explanation: Superlative adjectives compare three or more things. They show that something is the most or the greatest of all. For example: “The volcano is the most powerful natural event.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Short word (one syllable): add -est. tall → tallest, deep → deepest.
Word ending in -y: change y to i, add -est. foggy → foggiest.
Long word (two or more syllables): use most before it. exciting → most exciting.
Always put the before a superlative: the tallest, the foggiest.
Irregulars: good → best, bad → worst.
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “This is most foggy morning.” ✗
Fix: Add “the”, and use the right form: “This is the foggiest morning.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Think “super means the best!” A superlative always needs its friend the standing in front of it.
grammar.practice: Write the superlative form of the word in brackets. (Remember “the”.) | This is ______ (funny) film I have ever seen. | She is ______ (smart) student in our class. | That was ______ (exciting) match of the season. | This is ______ (foggy) morning of the year. Answer key: 1) the funniest, 2) the smartest, 3) the most exciting, 4) the foggiest.

grammar.title: Present Continuous
grammar.explanation: The present continuous describes an action happening right now. It makes your speaking lively: you can say exactly what is going on this moment. For example: “The deer is roaming the meadow.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use the correct form of to be + verb + -ing.
I am reading.
He / She / It is roaming. (“The storm is coming.”)
We / You / They are watching. (“The leaves are rustling in the rain.”)
Some verbs are not usually used this way (stative verbs): know, like, understand. We say “I know the answer”, not “I am knowing”.
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “He is play football.” ✗
Fix: Add -ing to the action word: “He is playing football.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Picture a photo of the action happening now — someone running or dancing. If you can see it happening, use am / is / are + -ing.
grammar.practice: Write the present continuous form of the verb in brackets. | The dog ______ (bark) at the gate. | I ______ (eat) my lunch. | They ______ (play) in the park. | The rain ______ (fall) on the roof. Answer key: 1) is barking, 2) am eating, 3) are playing, 4) is falling.

grammar.title: Present Simple (Facts)
grammar.explanation: The present simple is used for facts, habits and things that are always true — like science facts. For example: “Solar energy comes from the sun.” “Fur keeps animals warm.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
For I, you, we, they → use the base verb: “Birds fly south.”
For he, she, it → add -s or -es: “It rains.” “She watches the sky.”
Negatives use do not / does not: “Ice does not stay hard in the sun.”
Questions start with do / does: “Does hail fall from clouds?”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “Fur keep animals warm.” ✗
Fix: With it (fur), add -s: “Fur keeps animals warm.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: “He, she, it — add -s to fit!” When the subject is one person or thing, the verb gets its little -s.
grammar.practice: Write the correct present simple form of the verb in brackets. | The Earth ______ (move) around the sun. | Cats ______ (chase) mice. | The sun ______ (rise) in the east. | Solar power ______ (come) from the sun. Answer key: 1) moves, 2) chase, 3) rises, 4) comes.

grammar.title: The Modal Verb “can”
grammar.explanation: Can is a special helping verb. It tells us what is possible or what someone is able to do. For example: “A tornado can destroy houses.” “You can see moisture on leaves.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Subject + can + base verb (no -s, -ed or -ing).
Yes: “I can swim.”
No: “I cannot (can't) swim.”
Question: “Can you swim?” (Swap the order.)
Good news: can never changes. It stays “can” for I, you, he, she, it, we and they.
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “He cans play guitar.” ✗ Also: “I can playing.” ✗
Fix: “He can play guitar.” ✓ Keep the base verb after “can”.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of can as a little superhero: it gives the verb the power to happen — and superheroes never change their name!
grammar.practice: Complete each sentence with can + the verb in brackets. | I ______ (dance) very well. | They ______ (finish) their homework on time. | She ______ (see) the stars at night. | A storm ______ (damage) crops. Answer key: 1) can dance, 2) can finish, 3) can see, 4) can damage.

grammar.title: Wh- Questions, Prepositions of Place and Imperatives
grammar.explanation: These three patterns let you ask, locate and instruct. Wh- questions ask for information, prepositions of place say where something sits, and imperatives tell someone what to do right now.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Wh- words: what, where, when, why, who, how.
Question order: wh- word + helping verb + subject + verb. “Where does hail form?”
Match the wh- word to the answer: where for a place, when for a time, why for a reason.
Prepositions of place show the position between two things.
on — resting on a surface: “The bird is on the roof.”
under — below something: “The rabbit hides under a bush.”
in / inside — within a space: “We are inside the hall.”
next to — beside: “The lamp is next to the sofa.”
between — in the middle of two: “The ball is between the chairs.”
Imperatives use the base verb with no subject: “Go.” “Listen.”
Add don't for a negative order: “Don't run!” Add please to be polite: “Please sit down.”
Use Let's when you include yourself: “Let's move inside.”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “You are going where?” ✗
Fix: Put the wh- word first and swap the order: “Where are you going?” ✓
Mistake: “The cat is in the table.” ✗
Fix: Use on for something resting on a surface: “The cat is on the table.” ✓
Mistake: “You listen to me.” ✗
Fix: Drop the “you”, because the listener is already understood: “Listen to me.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Call what, where, when, why, who and how your “wonder words”. Then picture your room to test a position word, and remember an order needs no “you” — just the action.
grammar.practice: Part A. Write the correct wh- word to complete each question. | ______ causes rainbows? | ______ do you go to school — by bus or on foot? | ______ is your best friend? | ______ do you feel today? | Part B. Choose on, under, in, next to or between. | The cat is ______ the box. (it is inside) | The toy is ______ the table. (resting on top) | The chair is ______ the desk. (beside it) | The dog is lying ______ the tree. (below the branches) | Part C. Write the correct imperative form of the verb in brackets. | ______ (close) the door, please. | ______ (not touch) that! | ______ (help) your sister with her homework. | ______ (listen) carefully to the instructions. Answer key — Part A: 1) What, 2) How, 3) Who, 4) How. Part B: 1) in, 2) on, 3) next to, 4) under. Part C: 1) Close, 2) Don't touch, 3) Help, 4) Listen.

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Describe Today's Weather
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Look outside, then get ready to say:
“Today the weather is ______.” (foggy / sunny / rainy / windy)
“The sky looks ______.”
“It is a good day for ______.”
Record yourself. Check: Did you speak clearly? Did you use at least one weather word from this unit?
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my weather description with my adult helper and tell me whether my weather word was accurate.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Compare Two Things in Nature
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Practise comparing, using comparative adjectives:
“A canyon is deeper than a meadow.”
“A hurricane is stronger than a storm.”
“Today is foggier than yesterday.”
Now make three sentences of your own comparing two things you can see.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Check my three comparing sentences with an adult present and tell me if I used than correctly each time.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Guess the Weather
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Play with your AI tutor or your family:
One person thinks of a kind of weather but keeps it secret.
The others ask questions: “Is it hot?” “Can you see far?” “Does it make a loud noise?”
Keep asking until someone guesses: “Is it a storm?” Then swap turns.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Play Guess the Weather with me while an adult sits nearby, and keep score of my questions.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Weather Word Expert
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Choose six words from the Word Wall, such as canyon, hail and solar.
For each one, say a clear question and then answer it in a full sentence.
Model: “What is hail? Hail is small balls of ice that fall during a storm.”
Record all six pairs, then listen back and mark the clearest one.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Quiz me on six Word Wall words with an adult in the room, and correct my full-sentence answers.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Explain How a Storm Forms
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Explain to a listener how a storm forms and why hail can damage crops.
Give one reason with because, as Nora does at the science fair.
Then answer two follow-up questions from your listener without notes.
Model: “Hail falls from the clouds because water freezes high in the sky.”
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me two follow-up questions about storms while an adult listens, and check that I used because.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: Three-Minute Storm Safety Talk
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Plan a three-minute talk called “How to stay safe in a storm”.
Open with one sentence that says why the talk matters.
Give three safety ideas, each with an example from this unit.
Close by telling your listeners the one thing to remember.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Time my three-minute safety talk with an adult and tell me whether my three ideas stayed in order.

writing.title: Writing 1: A Weather Fact File
writing.promptAndInstructions: Choose one kind of powerful weather: a hurricane, a tornado, or a volcano. Write three or four fact sentences about it. Use the present simple for facts. For example: “A hurricane brings strong wind. It can knock down trees.”
writing.modelText: A hurricane forms over warm sea water. It brings heavy rain and very strong wind. It can lift roofs and knock down trees. People close their shutters and move away from the coast.
writing.successCriteria: I chose one kind of weather; I wrote three or four facts; every verb is in the present simple; I used two unit words; I checked capital letters and full stops.
writing.support: Say each fact aloud before you write it, and borrow a fact from the Reading or the story.
writing.extension: Add one sentence with can to say what that weather is able to do.

writing.title: Writing 2: Your Own Weather Poem
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write your own short poem called “The ______ Morning” (snowy, sunny, rainy, stormy). Use describing words for how it looks, sounds and feels, like the poem you read:
The morning air is ______ and ______, / The ______ have almost gone away. / ______, ______, ______ and ______ — / The whole world ______ below.
Then draw a picture to go with your poem.
writing.modelText: The morning air is crisp and white, / The rooftops have gone out of sight. / So bright, so silent, cold and deep — / The whole world rests in snowy sleep.
writing.expectedLength: Four poem lines plus a drawing
writing.successCriteria: I chose a weather word for my title; I filled every gap; I used describing words for sight, sound and feeling; my last line finishes the picture.
writing.support: Collect six describing words first, then try them in the gaps until they sound right.
writing.extension: Try a simile, such as “as quiet as fog”, in one of your lines.

writing.title: Writing 3: Storm Safety Instructions
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write five numbered instructions for a class poster called “What to do in a storm”. Start each one with an imperative verb, and use a place word such as inside, under or next to. For example: “Move inside the hall quickly.”
writing.modelText: 1. Watch the sky for dark clouds. 2. Move inside the nearest building. 3. Stay away from tall trees. 4. Sit next to an adult and stay calm. 5. Wait until the thunder has passed.
writing.successCriteria: Every line starts with a verb; no line begins with you; I used three different place words; my numbers run in a sensible order.
writing.support: Underline the imperative verbs in the story before you write your own.
writing.extension: Add one polite instruction that begins with please and one that begins with Let's.

writing.title: Writing 4: Compare Two Places in Nature
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write one paragraph that compares a canyon, a meadow and a bay. Use two comparative sentences with than and one superlative sentence with the. Finish by saying which place you would most like to visit, and why.
writing.modelText: A canyon is deeper than a meadow, and its steep walls hold a river at the bottom. A bay is calmer than the open sea, because land wraps around the water. Of the three, the canyon is the most exciting place to visit.
writing.expectedLength: One organised paragraph of five or six sentences
writing.successCriteria: I used than twice; I used one superlative with the; I named all three places; I gave a reason for my choice.
writing.support: Draw the three places first and label one difference on each drawing.
writing.extension: Add an irregular comparative such as better or worse to one sentence.

writing.title: Writing 5: Science Fair Diary Page
writing.promptAndInstructions: Imagine you stood beside Amal and Nora in the science tent. Write a diary page about the moment the storm returned. Use the present continuous for what is happening around you, and include what you can see, hear and feel.
writing.modelText: The wind is rising and the surface of the lake is rippling. Teacher Yasmin is calling us into the hall. Hail is bouncing on the ground beside my shoes, and my heart is beating fast.
writing.successCriteria: I used am, is or are with an -ing verb at least four times; I wrote about sight, sound and feeling; I kept the characters' names correct.
writing.support: Reread the paragraph where the wind picks up and note three actions happening at once.
writing.extension: End with one sentence in the past tense that says how the evening finished.

writing.title: Writing 6: Edit and Improve Your Fact File
writing.promptAndInstructions: Return to your Weather Fact File. Rewrite three sentences so they are clearer, add one sentence using can, and correct every capital letter, full stop and -s ending. Then explain in one sentence what you improved.
writing.modelText: First draft: The tornado spin fast. Improved: A tornado spins fast, and it can lift dust high into the sky. I fixed the missing -s and added what the tornado is able to do.
writing.sentenceStarter: The sentence I improved most is...
writing.expectedLength: Three revised sentences plus one comment
writing.successCriteria: I rewrote three sentences; I added one can sentence; every he, she or it verb ends in -s where it should; I explained one improvement.
writing.support: Read your draft aloud and mark every place where you paused or stumbled.
writing.extension: Swap with a partner and suggest one further improvement each.

activities.title: Activities 1: True or False (Nature Facts)
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write True or False. If it is false, write the correct answer.
A canyon is deeper than a meadow.
Solar energy comes from the moon.
Hail is made of small balls of ice.
A gentle storm is stronger than a hurricane.
activities.answerSummary: Items 1 and 3 are true; item 2 is false because solar energy comes from the sun; item 4 is false because a hurricane is the stronger storm.

activities.title: Activities 2: Match the Word to the Meaning
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Match each word to its meaning. Write the pairs (for example, 1–c).
1. meadow
2. hail
3. moisture
4. fur
a. small balls of ice that fall in a storm
b. a large field of grass and flowers
c. the soft hair that covers some animals
d. a small amount of water in the air
activities.answerSummary: The four correct pairs are 1–b, 2–a, 3–d and 4–c.

activities.title: Activities 3: Fill in the Blanks (Weather Around You)
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Today the weather is ______.
The kind of weather I like best is ______, because ______.
In a storm, the safest thing to do is ______.
One animal that has thick fur is the ______.
These are about you, so there is no single right answer — check your sentences with your AI tutor.
activities.answerSummary: Personal responses; each gap must be filled with a real weather or animal word inside a complete sentence.

quizzes.question: What does the word “breath” mean?
quizzes.options: A small amount of water in the air or on a surface. | The air you take in and let out of your lungs. | Small balls of ice that fall from the sky during a storm. | A large field of grass and flowers where animals graze.
quizzes.correctAnswer: The air you take in and let out of your lungs.
quizzes.explanation: Breath is the air your lungs take in and let out, as in “I took a deep breath”.

quizzes.question: What does the word “canyon” mean?
quizzes.options: A part of the sea or a lake that is partly surrounded by land. | The soft hair that covers some animals' bodies. | Covered with, or full of, snow. | A deep valley with steep sides, often with a river at the bottom.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A deep valley with steep sides, often with a river at the bottom.
quizzes.explanation: A canyon is a deep valley with steep sides, which is why it is deeper than a meadow.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from “The Storm and the Science Tent”: Nora sat down, catching her _____.
quizzes.explanation: Nora had just run to the hall, so she sat down catching her breath.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from “Weather Around the World”: Rain helps plants grow, because plants need _____.
quizzes.explanation: The text explains that rain matters to plants because plants need moisture.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses the comparative form correctly?
quizzes.options: A hurricane is strong than a storm. | A hurricane is stronger than a storm. | A hurricane is most strong than a storm. | A hurricane is the strongest than a storm.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A hurricane is stronger than a storm.
quizzes.explanation: One-syllable adjectives add -er, and than joins the two things being compared.

quizzes.question: Complete the sentence: This is _____ morning of the year.
quizzes.options: more foggy | foggier | the most foggiest | the foggiest
quizzes.explanation: Foggy ends in -y, so it becomes foggiest, and a superlative needs the in front of it.

quizzes.question: Which sentence states the fact correctly?
quizzes.options: Fur keep animals warm. | Fur keeping animals warm. | Fur keeps animals warm. | Fur are keeping animals warm.
quizzes.explanation: Fur behaves like it, so the present simple verb takes -s: fur keeps.

quizzes.question: Which question matches the answer “Solar power comes from the sun.”?
quizzes.options: Where does solar power come from? | Who uses solar power at the school? | When does solar power stop? | Why is solar power free?
quizzes.correctAnswer: Where does solar power come from?
quizzes.explanation: The answer names a place the power comes from, so the question needs where.

quizzes.question: Choose the correct preposition: The toy is _____ the table, resting on top.
quizzes.explanation: Something resting on top of a surface sits on it, not under or inside it.

quizzes.question: Which sentence is a correct imperative?
quizzes.options: You listen to me carefully. | Listen to me carefully. | Listening to me carefully. | To listen to me carefully.
quizzes.explanation: An imperative drops the subject and starts with the base verb, so Listen is right.

teacherNotes.note: Pre-teach hurricane, tornado and volcano with pictures before the story, because several learners will meet these weather words for the first time. Some children have lived through a severe storm, so introduce the science tent scene gently and let anyone step out of the discussion. An adult must sit with the learner for every AI tutor task and every recording; a child is never left alone with the device, and recordings stay inside the class space. Give feedback on complete sentences, on the -s ending in present simple facts, and on the word than in comparisons.

teacherNotes.noteType: Grammar answer key and tutor guidance
teacherNotes.note:
Grammar answers (teacher copy). Practice 1: bigger, easier, higher, deeper. Practice 2: the funniest, the smartest, the most exciting, the foggiest. Practice 3: is barking, am eating, are playing, is falling. Practice 4: moves, chase, rises, comes. Practice 5: can dance, can finish, can see, can damage. Practice 6 Part A: What, How, Who, How. Part B: in, on, next to, under. Part C: Close, Do not touch, Help, Listen.
Tutor guidance. Steer learners towards asking the tutor to compare moisture with sweat, to explain the difference between a hurricane and a tornado, to picture a canyon, a meadow and a bay, and to explain why metal rusts and food grows mould. For grammar, the most useful requests are more comparative sentences about weather and an explanation of he likes against I like. Every one of these requests is done with an adult sitting alongside.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Items 1 and 3 are true. Item 2 is false: solar energy comes from the sun, not the moon. Item 4 is false: a hurricane is far stronger than a gentle storm. Award the mark only when a false item is corrected.
The pairs are 1–b, 2–a, 3–d and 4–c. Watch for learners who swap moisture and fur, and ask them to reread both meanings aloud.
Personal responses. Accept any real weather word in gap 1, a reason after because in gap 2, a safe action such as going inside in gap 3, and any furred animal in gap 4.
Expected wording: What causes a hurricane? Where does hail form? Where does solar power come from? Accept any wh- word that genuinely fits the answer given.
Places: canyon, meadow, bay. Weather: storm, hail, hurricane, tornado, snowy. How Nature Works: volcano, rust, mould, roam. The rule sentences must name the shared idea, not simply list the words.

Expect six of these: walk slowly in fog, go inside when you hear thunder, move calmly rather than running, cover seedlings before hail, watch the sky for dark clouds, stay beside an adult. Each one must name its source text.
Correct answer: The air you take in and let out of your lungs. Breath is the air your lungs take in and let out, as in “I took a deep breath”.
Correct answer: A deep valley with steep sides, often with a river at the bottom. A canyon is a deep valley with steep sides, which is why it is deeper than a meadow.
Correct answer: breath Nora had just run to the hall, so she sat down catching her breath.
Correct answer: moisture The text explains that rain matters to plants because plants need moisture.
Correct answer: A hurricane is stronger than a storm. One-syllable adjectives add -er, and than joins the two things being compared.
Correct answer: the foggiest Foggy ends in -y, so it becomes foggiest, and a superlative needs the in front of it.
Correct answer: Fur keeps animals warm. Fur behaves like it, so the present simple verb takes -s: fur keeps.
Correct answer: Where does solar power come from? The answer names a place the power comes from, so the question needs where.
Correct answer: on Something resting on top of a surface sits on it, not under or inside it.
Correct answer: Listen to me carefully. An imperative drops the subject and starts with the base verb, so Listen is right.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Nature & Weather" — new words, a grammar focus, and a story. See exactly what they will practise below.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 8-9 years old and is building on English they already know. So YOU lead this unit alongside them — a teacher in class or a parent at home.

Work in short, regular sessions rather than one long one. Reading together, saying words out loud, and playing with the grammar patterns matter more than getting every answer right first time.

This guide tells you what the unit covers and how to go through it together. The learner's own pages (Reading & story, Grammar, Activities) are what your child works through on screen.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
The AI Tutor is there for extra practice and conversation — a grown-up should still be nearby, especially the first few times.

Ask the tutor to say a word slowly so your child can copy it: "Please say the word 'breath' slowly."

Ask it to make up a short question using this unit's words, or to listen to your child's sentence and say if it sounds right.

Ask it for one more practice question if your child wants to keep going after the unit is finished.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for teaching this unit
sections.body:
Keep sessions short and positive. Stop while it is still enjoyable, not after it has become a chore.

Say new words and example sentences out loud yourselves — hearing English spoken, not just reading it, is what builds confidence.

Let your child make mistakes without worrying. Gently model the correct version rather than correcting every slip.

Praise effort and progress, not just correct answers — confidence carries a learner further than perfect grammar at this stage.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Name and describe places in nature and different kinds of weather.
Compare two things using comparative adjectives (deeper, stronger, foggier).
Say which is the greatest using superlative adjectives (the deepest, the most powerful).
Describe what is happening now using the present continuous (“The storm is coming.”).
State facts about nature using the present simple (“Solar energy comes from the sun.”).
Say what is possible using can (“A tornado can destroy houses.”).
Ask and answer wh- questions about the weather.
Say where things are using prepositions of place, and give instructions with imperatives.
Explain simple ways to stay safe in a storm.

sections.title: Words We Will Learn
items: Water, Air and the Body: breath · sweat · moisture · surface · fur
Places in Nature: canyon · meadow · bay
Weather and Storms: storm · hail · hurricane · tornado · foggy · snowy
How Nature Works: volcano · solar · rust · mould · roam · royal

items: The Story — "The Storm and the Science Tent"
Reading — "Weather Around the World"
Reading — "A Poem: “The Foggy Morning”"

sections.title: How to Teach This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
Repeat this simple shape over one or two short sessions:

1. Warm-up (2-3 min)
Say hello in English together and ask what your child remembers from the last unit.

2. Learn the words (5-10 min)
Go through Water, Air and the Body, Places in Nature, Weather and Storms, How Nature Works, a few words at a time. Say each word, then have your child repeat it and use it in a short sentence.

3. Grammar and practice (5-10 min)
Look at "Comparative Adjectives" together and try a few lines of its practice out loud.

4. Story and listening time (5 min)
Read or listen to "The Storm and the Science Tent" together, and enjoy "The Weather Report" too.

5. Activity time (5-10 min)
Sit with your child and do "Activities 1: True or False (Nature Facts)" together, reading each instruction aloud for them if needed.

6. Wrap-up (2 min)
Ask what they learned today and celebrate with a “Well done!”

sections.title: Sentence Patterns to Say Out Loud
items: Always use than to join the two things you compare.
I am reading.
Birds fly south.
I can swim.
Where does hail form?

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. Just watch for these as you go through the unit together:
items: All twenty Word Wall words ticked, plus six weather and nature words used correctly in Speaking 4.
Two accurate than sentences in Writing 4 and three spoken comparisons in Speaking 2.
One correct superlative with the in Writing 4, plus Grammar Practice 2 completed accurately.
Four or more am / is / are + -ing verbs used correctly in the Writing 5 diary page.
Three or four accurate fact sentences in Writing 1 and a correct True or False set in Activities 1.
Grammar Practice 5 completed, plus one added can sentence in the Writing 6 revision.
Three correct questions written in Activities 4 and turn-taking questions recorded in Speaking 3.
Five imperative instructions with three different place words in the Writing 3 poster.
Six pieces of safety advice traced to their texts in Activities 6 and delivered in the Speaking 6 talk.
